about: Rules for a scene beat. Sources: the principal's notes (2026-10-07), the Masters of the Air study, scene-writing skill.

rules.q: What speed does this beat play at on screen?

criteria.fast: Fast action: quick cuts under about 1.5 s, things happening fast
criteria.slow: A slow held event: long holds, talk, waiting, dread
criteria.medium: In between: nothing fast, nothing held, a purposeless middle pace

rules.source: the principal: fast action or slow events, never a medium curve

rules.q: The beat's labelled speed (FAST or SLOW in the beat sheet row) matches the shot durations and the action written in the scene text.
The spoken lines are people answering and reacting to each other (replies, interruptions, cut-offs), not lines delivered to an audience.
rules.source: the principal: natural talk between two or more, never theatre

rules.q: A character explains the plot, the situation or their own feelings in full sentences for the audience's benefit.
While someone speaks, the coverage shows a listener or the thing being talked about, not only the speaker.
The beat has one clear thing the viewer must understand, and it happens on screen as a cause followed by a reaction.
Something changes between the start and the end of this beat (a situation, a decision, a position, a sound).
For every shot of this beat, the coverage states which way the people look or which way things move on screen.
rules.source: the principal: spatial logic is the most important thing in films

rules.q: Every shot of this beat states where we hear from (inside the aircraft, outside, intercom, radio, a speaker in open air), and that perspective fits where the camera is.
rules.source: reference study: inside vs outside, intercom vs radio

rules.q: How real does the professional talk and procedure sound to someone who does this job?
rules.source: the principal: everything on screen is real

rules.q: Every shot in this beat is something current AI video does well in 1-4 s (no long continuous acting, no fine hand work, no readable text, no crowd close-ups).
rules.source: scene-writing: writing for the models we have
